title: Project
text:
0.1 Introduction
This is an introduction to the project. This is also the landing page to your book if you chose to publish it. The purpose of this page is to introduce your reader to the project itself, perhaps provide some early documentation of the variables and values of your data, and any idiosyncracies of the analysis itself.

2.2 Data Import
Time to import my data and get to work!

df_raw <- read.csv("data/validation.csv", header = T)

# Create a sample dataframe
df <- data.frame(
  sex = c(1,2,1,2),
  pas = c(0,1,0,1)
)

df <- df %>% 
    set_variable_labels(
    sex = "Participant sex", 
    pas = "Passed test"
    ) %>%
    set_value_labels(
        sex = c(
            Male = 1, 
            Female = 2,
            Missing = -9
            ), 
        pas = c(
            Fail = 0, 
            Pass = 1
            )
            )

title: 5  Figures
text:
5.2 Data Visualization
Here’s a good spot to make some data visualizations for exploratory or event publication ready figures. Adding this reference to Figure 5.1 allows readers to hover over the refence to preview the figure which can be helpful if you have long blocks of text and are discussing a figure which may not appear for a while.
https://github.com/quarto-dev/quarto-cli/discussions/4655
If you’re just going to have an HTML document without a PDF, I’d recommend leaning on the embed-resources: true in the _quarto.yml file. When this is used, you don’t need to seperately store your figures and then display them using Markdown (e.g., ![]()). They can, insead, simply be labelled in the R code chunk itself (e.g., #| label: fig-1)

title: 5  Figures
text:
5.3 Simple Figure
Figure 5.1 is an example of a simple figure which can quickly be put together for exploratory purposes. You’ll notice the Figure 5.1 is automatically named when the document is numbered with the option numbered-sections: true in the _quarto.yml file. This is also the default. If you chose false the figure and cross-reference will be titled whatever is in the parenthesis.

fig1 <- ggplot(data = df, aes(x = lapr, y = factor(job_knowledge_quintile))) +
    geom_bar(stat = "summary", fun = mean, width = .5)

title: 5  Figures
text:
5.4 Publication Ready Figure
Figure 5.2 is a the same figure as above, just made a little more polished for publication.

fig2 <- ggplot(data = df, aes(x = lapr, y = factor(job_knowledge_quintile))) +
    geom_bar(stat = "summary", fun = mean, width = .5) +
    geom_text(aes(label = nround(after_stat(x),2)), 
                   stat = "summary", 
                   fun = "mean",
                   size = 20/.pt,
                   hjust = -.2) +
    coord_cartesian(xlim = c(1,5)) +
    labs(
        title = "Average Performance by Job Knowledge Quintile",
        x = "Average Last Annual Performance Review Rating",
        y = "Job Knowledge Test Quintile"
    ) +
    theme_minimal(base_size = 20) +
    theme(
        axis.text.x = element_blank(),
        axis.text.y = element_text(size = 20),
        panel.grid = element_blank()
        )

title: 5  Figures
text:
5.5 Figure Export
It’s often important to have figures in a format suitable for manuscripts or other programs. We also need to export the figures for later reference in markdown format using ![]().

ggsave(
    plot = fig1,
    filename = "figures/Figure1.png",
    height = 6.5,
    width = 10,
    units = "in"
    )

ggsave(
    plot = fig2,
    filename = "figures/Figure2.png",
    height = 6.5,
    width = 10,
    units = "in"
    )
